title: Consensus Algorithms Lecture
provenance: Synthetic transcript authored for this repository; no real meeting content.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Welcome to Introduction to Distributed Systems, lecture seven. Today we're covering consensus algorithms.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Consensus is fundamental to building reliable distributed systems. It allows multiple nodes to agree on a single value even in the presence of failures.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: The classic problem is called the Byzantine Generals Problem, first described by Lamport, Shostak, and Pease in nineteen eighty-two.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Imagine several generals surrounding a city, trying to coordinate an attack. They can only communicate via messengers, and some generals might be traitors.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: The challenge is: how can the loyal generals reach agreement on a plan when traitors might send false messages?

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: This maps directly to distributed systems where some nodes might fail or behave maliciously.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: There are two main types of failures we consider: crash failures and Byzantine failures.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Crash failures are when a node simply stops responding. This is the easier case to handle.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Byzantine failures are when a node sends arbitrary or malicious messages. Much harder to handle.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Let's look at Paxos, one of the most important consensus algorithms. Paxos was invented by Leslie Lamport.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Paxos has three roles: proposers, acceptors, and learners. A node can play multiple roles.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: The basic Paxos algorithm runs in two phases: the prepare phase and the accept phase.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: In the prepare phase, a proposer selects a proposal number and sends a prepare request to acceptors.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Acceptors respond with a promise not to accept proposals with lower numbers, and report any previously accepted values.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: In the accept phase, if the proposer receives promises from a majority, it sends an accept request with the proposal value.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Acceptors accept the proposal unless they've already promised a higher proposal number.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Once a majority of acceptors accept a proposal, consensus is reached and learners are notified.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: The key insight is that we only need a majority, not unanimity. This provides fault tolerance.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: If you have five nodes, you can tolerate two failures. With seven nodes, you can tolerate three failures.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Now let's discuss Raft, which was designed to be easier to understand than Paxos.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Raft was published by Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout in twenty fourteen.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Raft divides consensus into three subproblems: leader election, log replication, and safety.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: In Raft, one node is elected as leader. The leader handles all client requests and coordinates log replication.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Followers are passive and simply respond to leader requests. If a follower doesn't hear from the leader, it can become a candidate.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Leader election uses randomized timeouts to prevent split votes. This is simpler than Paxos's proposal numbers.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Once elected, the leader appends new entries to its log and replicates them to follower logs.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: An entry is committed once the leader has replicated it to a majority of nodes.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Raft guarantees that committed entries will eventually be executed by all available state machines.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Let me show you a comparison. Both Paxos and Raft provide the same safety guarantees, but Raft is generally considered more understandable.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Many production systems use Raft: etcd, Consul, CockroachDB. Fewer systems use pure Paxos, though Google's Chubby uses a Paxos variant.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: There's also practical Byzantine fault tolerance, or PBFT, which handles Byzantine failures.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: PBFT can tolerate up to one-third of nodes being Byzantine faulty. So with four nodes, you can tolerate one Byzantine node.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: PBFT is more expensive than crash-fault-tolerant algorithms because it requires more message rounds.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Blockchain systems use variations of Byzantine consensus. Bitcoin uses proof of work, which is a form of probabilistic consensus.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Ethereum is moving to proof of stake, which is more energy efficient than proof of work.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: For your homework, I want you to implement a basic Raft cluster with three nodes.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: The assignment is posted on the course website. It's due two weeks from today, on October twenty-fifth.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: You should implement leader election and basic log replication. Don't worry about log compaction yet.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: In the next lecture, we'll cover distributed transactions and the two-phase commit protocol.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: We'll also discuss the CAP theorem and why you can't have consistency, availability, and partition tolerance simultaneously.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Read the Raft paper before next class. It's very well written and includes excellent visualizations.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Any questions? Feel free to come to office hours on Wednesdays from two to four PM.

segments.speaker: Dr. Maria Santos
segments.text: Alright, that's all for today. See you next week!
